newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Washington's Albright charms old foes and friends.
newsitem.headline: Washington's Albright charms old foes and friends.

text.p: On a hectic first tour to Europe, Madeleine Albright -- America's first woman secretary of state -- won full marks for a charm offensive which delighted old friends and foes alike.

Chatting in French and Russia and swapping reminiscences of a youth spent in war-torn Europe, the Washington's number one diplomat succeeded in changing the atmosphere, if not any of the substance, of transatlantic diplomacy.
"It was a morale-boosting visit," said one senior diplomat at NATO's Brussels headquarters of the tour that took in Rome, Bonn, Paris, Brussels, London and Moscow.

Behind the kisses and backslapping, little progress was made, however, on resolving problems ranging from tensions over trade policy towards Cuba to how to proceed with NATO's planned eastwards expansion.

Most notable among the straight-talking Albright's achievements appeared to be setting a difficult relationship with France on a surer footing and the most positive meeting with Russian President Boris Yeltsin for several months.
Czech-born Albright charmed French leaders by speaking their language fluently and suggesting that Paris and Washington stop publicly squabbling "in front of the children".

France and the United States have been at loggerheads over plans to give Europeans more say in a revamped NATO with Paris calling for a European commander of the alliance's strategic southern command which includes the American Sixth Fleet.
Paris has also differed with Washington over the Middle East peace process, plans to enlarge NATO into former communist Europe, and how to strike a new post-Cold war deal with Russia.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, accused of snubbing her dour predecessor Warren Christopher, was clearly taken by the new secretary of state calling her a "very great lady who represents a very great country".
In an oblique reference to his problems with the understated Christopher, de Charette said: "It is always easier to talk with someone who speaks with sincerity and frankness."

The popular France-Soir said in an editorial: "After Madeleine Albright's brilliant entry onto the international stage, there is no danger of anyone forgetting the United States's status as a superpower, tempted by hegemony."

Some Europeans, angered by Washington's Helms-Burton act penalising European companies which trade with Cuba, fear America's emergence as the world's only superpower could tempt it to disregard the concerns of its allies.

In talks with senior European Union officials, Albright stressed all sides were united on the need to deal with President Fidel Castro and played down the differences over Helms-Burton, suggesting a way-out would be found.

In Bonn and Rome, Albright was also a big hit and after her visit to Moscow, Yeltsin said he was confident a compromise on the thorny issue of NATO's enlargement would be reached at a March summit with President Bill Clinton.
"This resolute woman is exactly to the taste of the chancellor. Helmut Kohl was impressed with her on their first meeting," said the Tagesspiegel daily in Berlin.

The press approvingly highlighted Albright's blunt criticism of the Church of Scientology for charging Germany treated its members like the Nazis did the Jews. She called the comparison "historically inaccurate and distasteful".
Albright, who was brought up a Christian, only learned last month that three of her Jewish grandparents were killed by the Nazis in the Holocaust.
